title: MLOps / Production AI
blurb: Model versioning, evaluation gates, drift, and safe rollout -- what makes a trained model a reliable production service, not just a notebook that worked once.

beginner: Why production AI is a different discipline
advanced: Model monitoring: what to actually track

description: Model versioning, evaluation gates, serving patterns, drift detection, canary rollout, and rollback -- the operational discipline that sits at the intersection of AI/ML and CI/CD.

lessons.title: Why production AI is a different discipline
objectives: Explain what changes once a model leaves a notebook and enters production
Explain how production AI changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect production AI with notebook vs production gap and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A model that scores well on a test set in a notebook is not yet a production system -- it's a promising result.
examples:
# the shift this course is about:
# notebook success: 'this model scored 94% on my test set'
# production reality: 'this model is currently serving real traffic, its input
# distribution is shifting, and I need to know the moment its real-world
# performance degrades -- not just its performance on a test set from last month'
commonMistakes: Treating a good test-set score as the finish line -- a model's real job starts once it's serving live traffic against data that will keep changing after that test set was frozen.
lessons.careerRelevance: This gap -- between 'the model works' and 'the model is a reliable production service' -- is exactly what separates ML research roles from AI/ML engineering roles.

lessons.title: Model versioning & the model registry
objectives: Explain what a model registry tracks and why version identity must be explicit
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: feature store awareness.
Explain how model registry changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect model registry with model versioning and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A model registry tracks every trained model as a versioned artifact -- not just the weights, but the training data version, the code/config that produced it, and its evaluation metrics, all tied to one identifiable version.
examples:
# what a registry entry actually captures:
# version: 'fraud-detector-v1.4.2'
# stage: 'production'
# trained_on: 'dataset-snapshot-2026-03-01'
# metrics: {accuracy: 0.94, precision: 0.91}
# -- every one of these fields answers a question you WILL need to answer later
commonMistakes: Treating a model file as just another file to overwrite when retrained -- without an explicit registry entry per version, you lose the ability to answer 'what exactly is running, and can we.
lessons.careerRelevance: MLflow, Weights & Biases, and SageMaker Model Registry are all real, widely-used implementations of exactly this idea. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Reproducible training runs
objectives: Explain what must be fixed/recorded for a training run to be genuinely reproducible
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: experiment tracking.
Explain how reproducibility changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect reproducibility with random seeds and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A reproducible training run means anyone (including future you) can rerun the exact same training process and get the same model -- requiring a fixed random seed, a pinned, recorded version of the training data (not just 'the data as of whenever'), and pinned library/dependency versions.
examples:
# reproducibility requires ALL of these fixed and recorded, not just one:
# random_seed = 42
# training_data_version = 'dataset-snapshot-2026-03-01'  -- not 'latest'
# library_versions = 'pinned in requirements.txt/lockfile'
# without ALL three, a training run genuinely cannot be reproduced later
commonMistakes: Training against 'the current data' with no fixed snapshot -- if the underlying data changes before you need to reproduce a training run, there's no way back to what actually happened.
lessons.careerRelevance: This directly extends the Data Science course's own reproducibility lesson, applied specifically to the training-run context. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.
lessons.explain: A reproducible training run means anyone (including future you) can rerun the exact same training process and get the same model -- requiring a fixed random seed, a pinned, recorded version of the training data (not just 'the data as of whenever'), and pinned library/dependency versions.

# library_versions = 'pinned in requirements.txt/lockfile'

lessons.title: Evaluation gates before deployment
objectives: Explain what an evaluation gate checks and why comparing to a fixed threshold alone is insufficient
Explain how evaluation gate changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect evaluation gate with absolute threshold and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An evaluation gate is an automated check a candidate model must pass before it's allowed to deploy -- similar in spirit to CI/CD's automated tests, but checking model quality metrics instead of code correctness.
examples:
# why BOTH comparisons matter:
# absolute limit only: a candidate barely above the floor could still be
# WORSE than what's currently in production -- and would pass anyway
# baseline-only: a candidate could match a baseline that was ALREADY too low
# checking both catches what either check alone would miss
commonMistakes: Comparing a candidate model only to an absolute threshold, never to the current production baseline -- this can let a real regression through if the threshold itself was set generously.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is directly the model-specific version of CI/CD's pipeline stages -- an automated gate a change must pass before it's allowed to ship.

lessons.title: Model serving patterns
objectives: Distinguish batch and online/real-time inference and when each fits
Explain how batch inference changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect batch inference with online/real-time inference and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Batch inference runs a model against a large set of inputs on a schedule (nightly, hourly), producing predictions ahead of when they're needed -- efficient, but predictions can be stale by the time they're used.
examples:
# choosing by the actual requirement:
# 'score every customer's churn risk once a month for a dashboard' -> batch
# (predictions can be a day old, no problem)
# 'flag this specific transaction as fraud RIGHT NOW, before it completes' -> online
# (a stale prediction here is actively useless)
commonMistakes: Defaulting to real-time serving for every use case 'to be safe' -- online serving adds real latency and availability requirements that batch inference simply doesn't need when the use case.
lessons.careerRelevance: This exact choice (batch vs online) is a common, concrete system-design question specifically for AI/ML infrastructure roles.

lessons.title: Latency, throughput & cost trade-offs in serving
objectives: Explain the batch-size and instance-tier trade-offs in model serving cost and latency
Explain how batching changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect batching with instance tier and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Serving infrastructure choices trade latency against cost in predictable ways: batching multiple requests together before running inference improves throughput and lowers cost-per-request, but adds latency (a request may wait briefly for a batch to fill).
examples:
# the trade-off, not a single 'right' answer:
# small batch, small instance: cheap per-hour, but higher latency and lower throughput
# large batch, large instance: lower latency per request, but costs more to run
# --> the correct choice depends on the use case's actual latency tolerance, not a universal rule
commonMistakes: Assuming 'bigger instance = better' universally -- for a use case that can tolerate some latency, a smaller, cheaper instance with batching is often the more sensible, cost-effective choice.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding this trade-off explicitly (not just picking the biggest available instance) is a genuine cost-optimization skill in real AI infrastructure roles.

lessons.title: Shadow deployment & champion/challenger testing
objectives: Explain shadow deployment and champion/challenger testing as two ways to safely evaluate a new model
Explain how shadow deployment changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect shadow deployment with champion/challenger testing and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Shadow deployment runs a new candidate model alongside the current production model on real traffic, but its predictions are only logged and compared -- never actually shown to users or acted on. This lets you observe real-world behavior with zero user-facing risk before trusting it with any real decisions.
examples:
# shadow deployment: challenger runs alongside champion, its output is
# logged and compared, but NEVER shown to users -- zero user-facing risk
# champion/challenger: challenger's predictions DO get used, but only for
# a small, controlled slice of real traffic -- some risk, but real signal
commonMistakes: Assuming shadow deployment and champion/challenger testing are the same thing -- shadow deployment carries zero user-facing risk (predictions are never acted on); champion/challenger does.
lessons.careerRelevance: Shadow deployment is a standard, low-risk first step before any real production model change at companies operating ML at scale.

lessons.title: Canary rollout for models
objectives: Apply the CI/CD canary concept specifically to model quality metrics, including sample-size caution
Explain how model canary rollout changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect model canary rollout with sample size and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: This directly extends CI/CD's canary deployment lesson: instead of gradually increasing traffic to a new SERVICE VERSION, you gradually increase traffic to a new MODEL VERSION, watching a model-quality metric (not just service health) as exposure increases.
examples:
# the model-specific caution CI/CD's generic canary lesson doesn't need:
# challenger tested on 10 requests, 9 correct -- looks great, but with only
# 10 samples this could easily be chance, not real quality
# -- treat this as INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE, not as a green light to promote,
# until a large enough sample has actually been observed
commonMistakes: Promoting a challenger model based on strong-looking early results from a tiny sample -- small samples can look great or terrible by pure chance; a real quality signal requires enough.
lessons.careerRelevance: This sample-size caution is exactly the kind of statistical judgment that distinguishes a careful MLOps practitioner from someone just wiring up a rollout mechanically.

lessons.title: Data drift & concept drift
objectives: Distinguish data drift from concept drift, and explain why a drift signal is a warning, not proof
Explain how data drift changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect data drift with concept drift and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Data drift means the INPUT data a model sees in production has statistically shifted from what it was trained on (e.g. customer demographics changed) -- the model's own logic hasn't changed, but the world feeding it has.
examples:
# same symptom (a drift score crossing a threshold), two different causes:
# data drift: the INPUTS changed (e.g. more mobile users than in training data)
# concept drift: the RELATIONSHIP changed (e.g. what 'fraud' looks like evolved)
# either way: drift is a signal worth INVESTIGATING, not proof the model is now wrong
commonMistakes: Treating any detected drift as automatic proof the model has gotten worse -- drift is a signal that something changed and deserves investigation; it doesn't by itself confirm real-world.
lessons.careerRelevance: Distinguishing data drift from concept drift (not just noticing 'something drifted') is a common, specific interview question for production ML roles.
lessons.explain: Data drift means the INPUT data a model sees in production has statistically shifted from what it was trained on (e.g. customer demographics changed) -- the model's own logic hasn't changed, but the world feeding it has.

lessons.title: Model monitoring: what to actually track
objectives: Name the categories of signal a production model monitoring setup should track
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: data validation / schema checks.
Explain how prediction distribution monitoring changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect prediction distribution monitoring with feature monitoring and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Beyond the drift signals from the previous lesson, production model monitoring typically tracks: prediction distribution (is the model suddenly predicting one class far more often than usual), input feature statistics (are individual features showing unexpected ranges or missing values), latency and error rates (is serving infrastructure itself healthy).
examples:
# monitoring categories, since no ONE metric is enough:
# prediction distribution -- is the mix of predicted classes shifting unexpectedly?
# input feature stats -- are individual features drifting or showing nulls?
# latency/error rate -- is the SERVING infrastructure itself healthy?
# ground-truth feedback (when available) -- were the predictions actually correct?
commonMistakes: Monitoring only infrastructure health (latency, uptime) and assuming that means the model itself is fine -- a model can be perfectly available and fast while its actual predictions have.
lessons.careerRelevance: This connects directly to the earlier Distributed Systems course's distributed-tracing lesson, applied specifically to what's worth tracking for a model rather than a general service. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Feedback loops & retraining triggers
objectives: Explain what should trigger a retrain, beyond just 'on a schedule'
Explain how feedback loop changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect feedback loop with retraining triggers and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A feedback loop closes the gap between a model's predictions and reality: capturing actual outcomes (did the customer actually churn, was the transaction actually fraudulent) and feeding them back to evaluate and eventually retrain the model.
examples:
# fixed-schedule-only retraining's blind spot:
# 'we retrain every month' -- but the model degraded significantly in week 2
# -- 3 weeks of degraded predictions before the scheduled retrain even starts
# metric/drift-based trigger: retrain as soon as monitored quality actually
# crosses a concerning threshold, not on an arbitrary calendar
commonMistakes: Relying purely on a fixed retraining schedule -- a model's actual degradation doesn't follow a calendar, and a purely time-based trigger can leave a genuinely degraded model in production.
lessons.careerRelevance: Designing sensible retraining triggers (not just 'whenever') is a real, recurring production-ML design decision.

lessons.title: A/B testing for ML-driven features
objectives: Explain what makes A/B testing an ML feature different from testing a model metric in isolation
Explain how A/B testing changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect A/B testing with business metric vs model metric and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A/B testing an ML-driven feature (e.g. a new recommendation model) measures its effect on a real BUSINESS metric (click-through rate, revenue, retention) by comparing two randomized user groups -- not just the model's own internal quality metric in isolation.
examples:
# why internal model metrics aren't the whole story:
# new recommendation model: 3% MORE accurate at predicting what a user will click
# A/B test result: revenue per user actually DECREASED slightly
# -- the internal metric improved, but the real business outcome didn't;
# only the A/B test on the real metric would have caught this gap
commonMistakes: Shipping a model purely because its internal quality metric improved, without an A/B test on the actual business outcome -- an improved proxy metric doesn't guarantee the real-world outcome.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is a frequently-cited real gap between 'the model got better' and 'the business actually benefited' -- a genuine, recurring lesson in production ML.
lessons.explain: A/B testing an ML-driven feature (e.g. a new recommendation model) measures its effect on a real BUSINESS metric (click-through rate, revenue, retention) by comparing two randomized user groups -- not just the model's own internal quality metric in isolation.

lessons.title: Rollback for models
objectives: Explain the compatibility checks a model rollback needs beyond CI/CD's code-and-schema concern
Explain how model rollback changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect model rollback with input schema compatibility and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: This directly extends CI/CD's rollback lesson (which covered code-and-database-schema compatibility) with concerns specific to models: rolling back to a previous model version also requires checking the INPUT SCHEMA it expects (has the format of incoming data changed since that version was retired).
examples:
# a model-specific rollback risk CI/CD's own rollback lesson doesn't cover:
# rolling back to model v1.2, which expects input_schema_v1 and preprocessing_v3
# but the CURRENT pipeline now produces input_schema_v2 and preprocessing_v4
# --> the OLD model is now silently fed data in a format it was never trained on
# even though the 'rollback' itself appeared to succeed
commonMistakes: Assuming a model rollback is safe as long as the model FILE itself is available -- the surrounding input schema, preprocessing, and feature pipeline must also still match what that older.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is precisely the kind of subtle, model-specific compatibility issue that separates genuine MLOps maturity from just having a model registry with old files in it.

objectives: Name the production concerns specific to LLM-based features, distinct from traditional ML models
Explain how LLM cost variability changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example

lessons.explanation: LLM-based features introduce concerns beyond traditional ML models: cost per request can vary significantly with prompt length and output length (unlike a fixed-cost traditional model inference), the exact model/prompt VERSION matters enormously since providers periodically update models even at a 'same' version string.

# LLM-specific production concerns, briefly:
# cost per request: varies with prompt+output length, unlike fixed-cost traditional inference
# version pinning: providers update underlying models over time -- pin explicitly,
# don't assume 'the same model name' means identical behavior forever
# output monitoring: needs relevance/safety signals, not just 'did it return without error'

lessons.title: The production-AI mindset
objectives: Synthesize the course's ideas into one core judgment: a shipped model is a liability without ongoing verification
Explain how production-AI mindset changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect production-AI mindset with ongoing verification and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Every idea in this course points to the same underlying shift: a trained model isn't a finished asset the moment it's deployed -- it's an ongoing responsibility that requires continuous verification, since the real world it's making predictions about keeps changing after training stopped.
examples:
# the reframe this whole course is building toward:
# NOT: 'we shipped the model, we're done'
# BUT: 'we shipped the model, and now we're responsible for knowing
# the moment it stops being right -- because the world it predicts about
# will keep changing after training stopped, whether we're watching or not'
commonMistakes: Treating model deployment as the finish line of an ML project -- deployment is closer to the starting line of the model's ACTUAL responsibility: staying correct against a world that keeps.
lessons.careerRelevance: This mindset -- treating a deployed model as an ongoing responsibility, not a finished deliverable -- is exactly what distinguishes mature MLOps practice from a one-time model handoff.

lessons.title: Precision, Quantization, and Serving Memory
objectives: Explain precision formats and quantization's memory/quality trade-off, and describe KV-cache and prefix caching as serving-memory concerns
Explain how precision formats (FP32/FP16/BF16/INT8) changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect precision formats (FP32/FP16/BF16/INT8) with post-training quantization and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Models are typically trained in FP32 (32-bit floating point) but served at lower precision to save memory and improve speed: FP16 and BF16 halve memory use with negligible quality impact for most models (BF16 additionally trades some precision for a wider numeric range, often more numerically stable during quantization).
examples:
# the SAME precision reduction applied to two DIFFERENT things:
# post-training quantization (this lesson): reduce precision of an ALREADY-
# TRAINED model specifically to serve it more cheaply/quickly
# QLoRA (Hugging Face's own coverage): quantize the frozen base model
# specifically to make TRAINING fit in less memory -- a different goal,
# a different point in the model's lifecycle, using the same underlying idea
commonMistakes: Assuming model weights are the only real memory cost in serving -- KV-cache grows with context length and concurrent request count, and can become the actual bottleneck even when the.
lessons.careerRelevance: Choosing an appropriate precision format and understanding KV-cache costs are concrete, practical decisions that directly determine how many concurrent users a given piece of serving hardware can actually support.

lessons.title: Measuring and Regression-Testing Inference Performance
objectives: Name the specific metrics used to measure inference performance, and design a regression check for a serving change
Explain how TTFT vs. tokens per second changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect TTFT vs. tokens per second with p50/p95/p99 latency and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Inference performance has its own specific vocabulary, distinct from general latency: time to first token (TTFT) measures how long a user waits before seeing any output at all, while tokens per second measures how fast generation proceeds once it starts -- a system can have excellent TTFT but slow tokens-per-second, or vice versa.
examples:
# TTFT and tokens-per-second measure genuinely DIFFERENT things:
# TTFT: how long before the user sees ANY output -- matters most for how
# responsive the experience FEELS at the start
# tokens/sec: how fast generation proceeds once started -- matters most for
# how long a LONG response takes to fully complete
# a system can excel at one while being mediocre at the other
commonMistakes: Reporting only an average latency number for an inference service -- p95/p99 tail latency reveals a meaningfully worse experience for a real subset of users that an average alone hides.
lessons.careerRelevance: TTFT and tokens-per-second specifically (not just generic 'latency') are exactly the metrics real production LLM-serving teams track and report on.
lessons.explain: Inference performance has its own specific vocabulary, distinct from general latency: time to first token (TTFT) measures how long a user waits before seeing any output at all, while tokens per second measures how fast generation proceeds once it starts -- a system can have excellent TTFT but slow tokens-per-second, or vice versa.
lessons.example:
# TTFT and tokens-per-second measure genuinely DIFFERENT things:
# TTFT: how long before the user sees ANY output -- matters most for how
# responsive the experience FEELS at the start
# tokens/sec: how fast generation proceeds once started -- matters most for
# how long a LONG response takes to fully complete
# a system can excel at one while being mediocre at the other

quiz.q: What distinguishes production AI from a good result in a notebook?
options: Nothing, a good score is the finish line
Production AI requires versioning, reproducibility, serving, and ongoing verification against changing real data
Production AI only matters for large companies
Notebooks are always more accurate

quiz.q: What does a model registry track beyond the model weights?
options: Nothing else is needed
Training data version, code/config, and evaluation metrics tied to one identifiable version
Only the file size
The developer's name

quiz.q: What three things must be fixed/recorded for a training run to be reproducible?
options: Only the code
Random seed, training data version, and pinned dependency versions
Only the random seed
The time of day training ran

quiz.q: Why should an evaluation gate compare a candidate against BOTH an absolute limit and the production baseline?
options: It shouldn't, one check is enough
Checking only one can let a genuinely worse model through, or block a fine one for the wrong reason
Absolute limits are never useful
Baselines are never useful

quiz.q: What's the key difference between batch and online (real-time) inference?
options: They are identical
Batch runs on a schedule and can be stale; online runs on-demand but adds latency and requires constant availability
Batch is always better
Online inference has no latency cost

quiz.q: What's the trade-off of batching multiple requests together before inference?
options: No trade-off exists
Improves throughput and lowers cost-per-request, but adds latency waiting for the batch to fill
It always makes everything faster
Batching only affects cost, never latency

quiz.q: What distinguishes shadow deployment from champion/challenger testing?
options: They are identical
Shadow deployment's predictions are only logged, never acted on; champion/challenger DOES act on the challenger's predictions for a limited traffic slice
Shadow deployment is riskier
Champion/challenger never uses real traffic

quiz.q: Why is a strong early result from a tiny canary sample not a reliable signal?
options: It always is reliable
A small sample can look great or terrible by pure chance, not a real quality difference
Small samples are always worse
Canary rollouts don't use samples

quiz.q: What's the difference between data drift and concept drift?
options: They are identical
Data drift is a shift in input data; concept drift is a shift in the actual input-output relationship
Data drift only affects images
Concept drift never happens in production

quiz.q: What does a detected drift signal actually prove?
options: That model quality has definitely decreased
It's a warning worth investigating, not proof that real-world quality has actually dropped
Nothing, drift signals are meaningless
That the model needs to be deleted

quiz.q: Why is monitoring only latency/uptime insufficient for a production model?
options: It's fully sufficient
A model can be perfectly available and fast while its actual predictions have silently become wrong
Latency is the only thing that matters
Uptime and prediction quality are the same thing

quiz.q: Why is a purely fixed-schedule retraining trigger risky?
options: It's never risky
A model can degrade faster than the schedule catches, leaving degraded predictions in production for weeks
Fixed schedules are always optimal
Retraining should never be triggered by metrics

quiz.q: Why does A/B testing an ML feature on a real business metric matter, beyond the model's own internal metric?
options: It doesn't matter, internal metrics are enough
A model can improve on its own metric while the actual business outcome doesn't improve or gets worse
A/B testing is only for websites
Internal metrics always predict business outcomes

quiz.q: What model-specific compatibility must a rollback check beyond code/database schema?
options: Nothing extra is needed
Input schema, preprocessing version, and feature availability the older model version expects
Only the model's file size
The model's original training date

quiz.q: What LLM-specific production concern differs from traditional ML models?
options: Nothing is different
Cost can vary significantly with prompt/output length, and providers may update models even at a stable version string
LLMs never need monitoring
LLM costs are always fixed

quiz.q: What is the core mindset shift this course argues production AI requires?
options: A deployed model is a finished asset needing no further attention
A deployed model is an ongoing responsibility requiring continuous verification, since the real world keeps changing
Models never need to be retrained
Deployment is the final step of an ML project

quiz.q: Why must model versioning be explicit, not just 'the latest trained model'?
options: It doesn't need to be explicit
Without an explicit, unambiguous version, you can't reliably answer what's actually running or reproduce it later
Explicit versioning slows down training
Only production models need versions

quiz.q: Why compare a canary model's traffic-based quality metric, not just its offline test-set score?
options: Offline scores are always sufficient
Real production traffic and offline test data can differ, and a canary directly observes real-world behavior before full rollout
Canary rollouts don't use quality metrics
Offline testing is unnecessary once a canary exists

quiz.q: Why keep MLOps content focused on operational judgment rather than modeling math?
options: Math is unimportant to AI overall
This course's purpose is the operational discipline of running models reliably, distinct from the modeling theory covered elsewhere
Operational skills are less valuable than math
There's no difference between the two focuses

quiz.q: Why does this course cross-reference CI/CD's deployment strategies rather than re-explaining them from scratch?
options: To avoid duplicating content already covered, while extending it with model-specific concerns
Because CI/CD's concepts don't apply to models at all
Because deployment strategies are unrelated to MLOps
Cross-referencing is only done for unrelated topics

quiz.q: What is the main trade-off of using INT8 precision instead of FP32 for serving?
options: No trade-off exists
Quartered memory use and increased throughput, at a small but measurable, task-dependent accuracy cost
INT8 always improves accuracy
INT8 only affects training, not serving

quiz.q: Why can KV-cache become a serving memory bottleneck even when the quantized model fits comfortably?
options: KV-cache never uses meaningful memory
KV-cache grows with context length and concurrent request count, independent of the model weights' own memory footprint
KV-cache size is fixed regardless of usage
Only unquantized models have a KV-cache

quiz.q: What is the key difference between time to first token (TTFT) and tokens per second?
options: They measure the exact same thing
TTFT measures how long until any output appears; tokens per second measures how fast generation proceeds once it has started
Tokens per second is always more important to measure
TTFT only matters for batch inference

exercises.title: Diagnose a reproducibility gap
exercises.prompt: A team retrains a model 'on the latest data' with no fixed data snapshot recorded. Months later, results look different and nobody can explain why. What's missing, and what would you add?
exercises.hint: a fixed, recorded training-data snapshot version -- without it, there's no way to tell whether the data changed, making the discrepancy impossible to diagnose

exercises.title: Design an evaluation gate for two metric directions
exercises.prompt: Design an evaluation gate for a fraud model that must check accuracy (higher is better) AND latency (lower is better). What should it compare each metric against?
exercises.hint: both metrics should be compared against an absolute limit AND the current production baseline -- checking only one direction of comparison can let a regression through

exercises.title: Choose batch or online inference
exercises.prompt: A team needs to score every user's monthly churn risk for an internal dashboard, versus flagging a specific transaction as fraud before it completes. Which serving pattern fits each, and why?
exercises.hint: churn risk -> batch (staleness is fine); fraud flagging -> online (a stale prediction is actively useless here)

exercises.title: Diagnose a canary sample-size mistake
exercises.prompt: A team promotes a challenger model to full production after it went 9-for-10 in a canary test. What's the actual risk in this decision?
exercises.hint: 10 samples is far too small to trust -- a 9/10 result could easily happen by chance even for a genuinely worse model; this should have been treated as insufficient evidence, not a green light

exercises.title: Distinguish data drift from concept drift
exercises.prompt: A fraud model's drift monitor fires. Investigation shows fraudsters have started using new tactics the model was never trained to recognize -- the input data format itself hasn't changed. Is this data drift or concept drift, and why?
exercises.hint: concept drift -- the relationship between inputs and the correct answer changed (what counts as fraud evolved), even though the input data format itself is unchanged

exercises.title: Explain why drift isn't proof of degradation
exercises.prompt: A colleague sees a drift alert and immediately assumes the model must be performing worse. How would you correct this framing?
exercises.hint: drift is a warning signal worth investigating, not proof by itself -- some drift is harmless, and metrics can be noisy; it needs actual investigation before concluding quality dropped

exercises.title: Design a monitoring plan beyond latency
exercises.prompt: A team only monitors their model's serving latency and uptime. List at least 2 additional signal categories they're missing, and why each matters.
exercises.hint: prediction distribution (is the mix of predicted classes shifting unexpectedly) and input feature statistics (are features drifting or showing nulls) -- both can reveal a model quietly going wrong even while latency/uptime look perfectly healthy

exercises.title: Design a retraining trigger
exercises.prompt: A team currently retrains 'every month, regardless.' Propose a better-designed trigger and explain the specific risk it addresses.
exercises.hint: a metric- or drift-based trigger (retrain when monitored quality drops below a threshold) -- addresses the risk of a model degrading faster than a fixed schedule catches, leaving degraded predictions live for weeks

exercises.title: Diagnose an A/B testing gap
exercises.prompt: A new recommendation model is 3% more accurate on its internal test set, so the team ships it without an A/B test. Revenue per user quietly decreases afterward. What went wrong in the decision process?
exercises.hint: the internal accuracy metric is a proxy, not the actual business outcome -- an A/B test on the real business metric (revenue) would have caught the gap between 'more accurate' and 'actually better for the business' before a full rollout

exercises.title: Diagnose a model rollback risk
exercises.prompt: A team rolls back to model v1.2 after a bad deploy. The model file loads successfully, but predictions become nonsensical. The current preprocessing pipeline has since been upgraded to preprocessing_v4, while v1.2 was trained expecting preprocessing_v3. What happened, and what should the rollback process have checked?
exercises.hint: the rolled-back model is being fed data preprocessed in a format it was never trained on -- the rollback process should have checked preprocessing-version compatibility (and input schema, and feature availability) before considering the rollback complete, not just restored the model file

exercises.title: Design a shadow deployment plan
exercises.prompt: You want to evaluate a new fraud-detection model with zero risk to real users before trusting it with any real decisions. Describe how shadow deployment would work here.
exercises.hint: run the new model alongside the current production model on real traffic; log and compare its predictions, but never act on them or show them to users -- purely observational until enough confidence is built

exercises.title: Compare champion/challenger to full A/B rollout
exercises.prompt: How does a champion/challenger test differ from immediately routing 50% of traffic to a new model?
exercises.hint: champion/challenger typically starts with a small, controlled traffic slice to the challenger (limiting exposure/risk), gradually increasing only as confidence builds -- rather than an immediate large-scale traffic split

exercises.title: Justify a latency-cost trade-off
exercises.prompt: A team is deciding between a small, cheap instance with batching (higher latency, lower cost) and a large instance with no batching (lower latency, higher cost) for a use case that tolerates up to 2 seconds of latency. Which would you recommend, and why?
exercises.hint: the small, cheaper batched option -- since the use case explicitly tolerates the added latency, there's no real benefit to paying for the lower-latency option

exercises.title: Identify an LLM-specific production concern
exercises.prompt: A team assumes their LLM-based feature's cost will stay constant like a traditional model's fixed inference cost. What's wrong with this assumption?
exercises.hint: LLM cost varies significantly with prompt length and output length, unlike a traditional model's roughly fixed per-inference cost -- this needs to be monitored, not assumed constant

exercises.title: Explain why model versioning must be explicit
exercises.prompt: A team says 'we're running the latest model' with no specific version identifier recorded anywhere. What problem does this create?
exercises.hint: there's no precise, unambiguous answer to what's actually running in production, and no way to reproduce or roll back to that exact version later

exercises.title: Design a feedback loop
exercises.prompt: Design a feedback loop for a loan-approval model where the true outcome (did the borrower default) is only knowable months later. What does this delay mean for retraining triggers?
exercises.hint: ground-truth feedback here is inherently delayed, so purely outcome-based retraining triggers can't react quickly; drift-based signals (input distribution changes) become more important as an earlier warning, since true-outcome feedback lags by design

exercises.title: Apply the CI/CD-to-MLOps extension
exercises.prompt: Explain, in your own words, how canary rollout for models extends CI/CD's canary deployment concept rather than duplicating it.
exercises.hint: CI/CD's canary tracks service health/traffic percentage for a new service version; the model-specific version tracks the SAME traffic-percentage mechanism but watches a model-quality metric instead, plus adds the sample-size caution that a service-health canary doesn't need

exercises.title: Synthesize the production-AI mindset
exercises.prompt: A colleague says 'the model is deployed, the project is done.' Using this course's own framing, explain what's missing from that view.
exercises.hint: deployment is closer to the start of the model's real responsibility, not the finish line -- the model now needs ongoing verification (drift, monitoring, evaluation gates on any future change) since the real world it predicts about keeps changing after training stopped

exercises.title: Choose a Precision Format for a Stated Requirement
exercises.prompt: A team needs the lowest possible memory footprint for a model serving many concurrent users, and can tolerate a small, measurable accuracy loss. Which precision format fits best?
exercises.hint: INT8 -- it quarters memory use and meaningfully increases throughput, at exactly the kind of small, measurable accuracy cost this scenario states is acceptable

exercises.title: Diagnose a KV-Cache Memory Exhaustion
exercises.prompt: A serving system runs out of memory under high concurrency, even though the quantized model itself fits comfortably. What's the likely cause?
exercises.hint: KV-cache exhaustion -- the attention mechanism's cached state grows with context length and concurrent request count, and can become the actual memory bottleneck independently of the model weights' own footprint

exercises.title: Interpret a p95 vs. p50 Latency Regression
exercises.prompt: After a serving change, p50 latency stayed the same but p95 latency doubled. What does this suggest, and why does it matter?
exercises.hint: a tail-latency regression affecting a smaller subset of requests -- the median user experience looks unchanged, but a real fraction of users now have a meaningfully worse experience the p50 number alone would completely hide

interviewPreparation.q: Why is a good test-set score not the same as a production-ready model?
interviewPreparation.a: Production AI requires versioning and reproducibility (knowing exactly what's running and being able to reproduce it), reliable serving under real traffic, and ongoing monitoring against real-world data that keeps changing after the test set was frozen -- a test-set score is a snapshot, not an ongoing guarantee.

interviewPreparation.q: Why should an evaluation gate compare a candidate model against both an absolute limit and the current production baseline?
interviewPreparation.a: Checking only an absolute limit can let a candidate through that's still worse than what's currently live, since the limit itself may have been set generously. Checking only the baseline risks anchoring to a baseline that was already too low. Comparing against both catches what either check alone would miss.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the difference between data drift and concept drift, and why does it matter which one you're seeing?
interviewPreparation.a: Data drift is a shift in the input data's distribution (the world feeding the model changed) with the true input-output relationship unchanged. Concept drift is a shift in that actual relationship itself (what counts as the correct answer has changed), even if the input data looks similar. They call for different responses -- data drift might just need monitoring, while concept drift usually requires retraining with data reflecting the new relationship.

interviewPreparation.q: Why is a strong canary result from a very small sample not a reliable signal to promote a model?
interviewPreparation.a: A small sample can look great or terrible purely by chance, independent of the model's real quality. Treating an early lucky (or unlucky) streak as a real signal risks promoting a genuinely worse model or blocking a genuinely better one based on noise rather than evidence -- a sufficient sample size is needed before the result can be trusted.

interviewPreparation.q: What compatibility checks does a model rollback need that a typical code rollback doesn't?
interviewPreparation.a: Beyond code and database schema compatibility, a model rollback needs to verify the input schema the older model version expects still matches what's currently produced, that the current preprocessing pipeline version still matches what that model was trained against, and that all features it needs are still being computed -- restoring the model file alone doesn't guarantee any of this.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you decide on a quantization precision for a production model?
interviewPreparation.a: Weigh the memory/throughput gains of a lower precision (FP16/BF16 for near-zero quality impact, INT8 for larger gains with a small measurable accuracy cost) against the specific task's tolerance for that accuracy loss -- there's no universally correct precision, it depends on the concurrency and latency requirements versus how much quality loss the task can actually absorb.

interviewPreparation.q: How do you detect an inference performance regression after a serving change?
interviewPreparation.a: Compare baseline and candidate runs across TTFT, tokens per second, p95 latency, throughput, and memory -- not just an average latency number, since a regression can hide in the tail (p95/p99) while the median looks completely unaffected.

capstone.title: Design and Simulate a Safe Model Deployment Pipeline
capstone.description: Design an end-to-end model deployment pipeline: a versioned model registry, an evaluation gate a candidate must pass before deployment, a rollout strategy with an honest justification, a monitoring plan naming specific drift and quality signals to track, and a rollback plan that explicitly checks model-specific compatibility (input schema, preprocessing version, feature availability), not just the ability to redeploy an old model file.
deliverables: A model registry design tracking version, stage, training data snapshot, and evaluation metrics for each version
An evaluation gate comparing a candidate against both an absolute limit and the current production baseline, for at least one higher-is-better and one lower-is-better metric
A chosen rollout strategy (shadow, champion/challenger, or canary) with a specific justification tied to this system's actual risk tolerance -- not just 'this is standard practice'
A monitoring plan naming specific signals (prediction distribution, feature statistics, drift score) rather than a generic 'we will monitor the model'
A rollback plan explicitly addressing model-specific compatibility -- input schema, preprocessing version, and feature availability -- not just restoring a previous model file
A short section identifying at least 2 things deliberately kept simple or manual in this design, and why full automation wasn't the right call there yet
capstone.portfolioTips: The rollback plan's model-specific compatibility checks are the detail that most separates 'I understand MLOps concepts' from 'I understand the actual failure modes' -- most candidates only think about restoring the model file itself.

industryUsage.usage: Runs extensive shadow deployment and champion/challenger testing for recommendation models before any production traffic is fully committed to a new model version.
Both are widely-used real implementations of the model registry concept covered in this course -- versioning, metadata, and stage promotion as a first-class practice.
SageMaker Model Monitor implements exactly the drift-detection and prediction-distribution monitoring concepts covered in this course as a managed production service.

careerApplications: Used by ML/AI and platform engineers to version data/models, track experiments, validate pipelines, deploy models, monitor production behavior, and reproduce training or inference results.
